stem: A teammate types `docker-compose up` and you type `docker compose up`. What is the practical difference today?

options.text: `docker-compose` is the new Go rewrite and `docker compose` is the legacy Python tool
options.why: It is the other way round: the hyphenated command is the retired v1 tool.

options.text: `docker compose` is Compose v2, a Docker CLI plugin; `docker-compose` is the retired v1 tool
options.why: Compose v2 ships as a CLI plugin, and v1 (Python) no longer receives updates.

options.text: They are the same binary, so the only difference is which shell alias you prefer
options.why: They are different programs: v1 was a standalone Python app, v2 is a Go plugin.

options.text: `docker compose` only works with Swarm clusters, while `docker-compose` targets a single local Docker engine
options.why: Both target a local Docker Engine; Swarm stacks use `docker stack deploy` instead.

explanation: Compose v2 is a Docker CLI plugin invoked as `docker compose`. The original Python `docker-compose` (v1) reached end of life and no longer receives updates. Some systems install a `docker-compose` shim that forwards to v2, but new scripts and docs should use `docker compose`. One visible change: v2 names containers with hyphens (`myapp-web-1`) instead of underscores.
reference: Docker docs: Migrate to Compose v2

stem: In a modern Compose project, the top-level `version: "3.8"` line selects which Compose file schema Docker Compose v2 uses to validate the file.

options.text: True
options.why: Compose v2 ignores the value for validation and always uses the latest Compose Specification schema.

options.text: False
options.why: The `version` key is obsolete and only informative; Compose prints a warning when it is present.

explanation: The top-level `version` property is kept only for backward compatibility. Compose always validates against the most recent Compose Specification schema and warns that `version` is obsolete. You can delete the line.
reference: Compose file reference: Version and name top-level elements

stem:
In this project, how should the `api` container connect to the database?

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
```

options.text: `postgres://localhost:5433`, the port published on the host
options.why: `localhost` inside the api container is the api container itself, not the host.

options.text: `postgres://db:5432`, the service name and the container port
options.why: Services on the default network resolve each other by service name and use container ports.

options.text: `postgres://db:5433`, the service name and the published port
options.why: Published ports are for clients outside the network; inside it, Postgres listens on 5432.

options.text: The container's IP address, which you look up with `docker inspect`
options.why: Container IPs change when containers are recreated; the service name stays stable.

explanation: Compose attaches every service to a default `<project>_default` network and registers each service name in its DNS. Containers reach each other by service name on the container port (`db:5432`). The published host port (5433) is only for clients outside that network, such as tools on your laptop.
reference: Docker docs: Networking in Compose

stem: Match each `depends_on` setting with its effect.

options.text: Waits only until the dependency container has started
options.why: The default condition.

options.text: Waits until the dependency's healthcheck reports healthy
options.why: Needs a `healthcheck` on the dependency.

options.text: Waits until the dependency exits with code 0
options.why: Useful for one-shot jobs such as migrations.

options.text: Only warns if the dependency is not started or available
options.why: Makes the dependency optional.

explanation: The short `depends_on` syntax equals `service_started`: Compose starts dependencies first but does not wait for them to be ready. `service_healthy` waits for a passing healthcheck, and `service_completed_successfully` waits for a one-shot container to exit with 0. `required: false` (Compose 2.20+) turns a missing dependency into a warning.
reference: Compose file reference: depends_on

stem: You run `docker compose up` with no `-f` flag in a folder that contains `compose.yaml`. Which other file name does Compose automatically merge on top of it, if it exists in the same folder? Type the file name.
explanation: Without `-f`, Compose looks for `compose.yaml` and, at the same directory level, `compose.override.yaml`, and merges the override on top. That is the conventional place for development-only settings such as bind mounts and debug ports. The legacy names `docker-compose.yml` and `docker-compose.override.yml` are still recognised.
reference: Docker docs: Merge Compose files

stem: A service lists `expose: ["9090"]` and has no `ports` entry. Who can connect to port 9090?

options.text: Any machine on the network, because `expose` publishes it on all host interfaces
options.why: Publishing to the host is what `ports` does; `expose` never publishes.

options.text: Only processes on the Docker host, through `localhost:9090`
options.why: Nothing is bound on the host, so `localhost:9090` on the host reaches nothing.

options.text: Other containers on the same Compose network, but not the host
options.why: `expose` documents an internal port; it is reachable only from containers on shared networks.

options.text: Nobody, until the service also sets `network_mode: host`
options.why: Containers on the same network can already reach it; host networking is unrelated.

explanation: `expose` declares ports for other containers on shared networks and does not publish them to the host machine. To reach a port from the host or the outside world, you need `ports` (for example `"9090:9090"`). On a user-defined network, containers can reach each other's listening ports even without `expose`; it mainly documents intent.
reference: Compose file reference: expose

stem: You run `docker compose down` with no options. Which two things does it remove? (Choose two.)

options.text: The containers for the project's services
options.why: `down` stops and removes the service containers.

options.text: The project's default network
options.why: Networks Compose created for the project, including `<project>_default`, are removed.

options.text: Named volumes declared under the top-level `volumes` key
options.why: Named volumes survive `down`; you need `down -v` to remove them.

options.text: The images built from the services' `build` sections
options.why: Images are kept unless you pass `--rmi`.

options.text: Networks declared with `external: true`
options.why: External networks are never removed by Compose, because it did not create them.

explanation: `docker compose down` stops and removes containers and the networks Compose created. Named volumes, images and external resources are kept, so your database data survives a plain `down`. Add `-v` to remove named and anonymous volumes, and `--rmi` to remove images.
reference: Docker CLI reference: docker compose down

stem: A service is given a Compose secret named `db_password`, defined from the file `./secrets/db_password.txt`. Where does the application read it inside the container by default?

options.text: From the environment variable `DB_PASSWORD`
options.why: Secrets are not injected as environment variables, which is the point: env vars leak easily.

options.text: From the file `/run/secrets/db_password`
options.why: Compose mounts each secret as a read-only file under `/run/secrets/<name>`.

options.text: From the file `/etc/secrets/db_password.txt`
options.why: Neither the directory nor the original file name is used; the target is `/run/secrets/<name>`.

options.text: From `docker secret inspect`, run inside the container
options.why: That command manages Swarm secrets from the CLI; apps read the mounted file.

explanation: Compose mounts secrets as files at `/run/secrets/<secret_name>`. Many official images support a `_FILE` variant of their variables for this, such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password`. Files avoid the leaks that environment variables suffer, for example through `docker inspect`, crash dumps or child processes.
reference: Docker docs: Manage secrets securely in Docker Compose

stem:
Which value does `NODE_ENV` have inside the container?

```yaml
# webapp.env contains: NODE_ENV=test
services:
  webapp:
    image: webapp
    env_file:
      - ./webapp.env
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
```

options.text: `test`, because `env_file` is applied after `environment`
options.why: The order is the other way: `environment` overrides values loaded from `env_file`.

options.text: `production`, because `environment` beats `env_file`
options.why: When both set a variable, the `environment` attribute wins.

options.text: Whatever the image's `ENV NODE_ENV` says
options.why: Both Compose attributes override the image's `ENV` defaults.

options.text: Compose refuses to start because the variable is defined twice
options.why: Defining a variable in both places is allowed; precedence decides the value.

explanation: For the container environment, Compose applies a precedence order. `docker compose run --env` comes first, then the `environment` attribute, then `env_file`, then the image's `ENV`. Here `environment` sets `production`, which overrides `test` from the env file.
reference: Docker docs: Environment variables precedence

stem: The project folder has a `.env` file containing `API_KEY=abc123`. The `api` service currently has no `environment` or `env_file` entries, and `echo $API_KEY` inside the container prints nothing. Which two changes make the variable available inside the container? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add `environment: [API_KEY=${API_KEY}]` to the service
options.why: The `.env` value is interpolated into the Compose file and then set in the container.

options.text: Add `env_file: .env` to the service
options.why: `env_file` loads every line of that file into the container environment.

options.text: Run `docker compose --env-file .env up` instead
options.why: `--env-file` only changes which file feeds interpolation; it still sets nothing in containers.

options.text: Rename the file to `compose.env` so Compose loads it for containers
options.why: No file name makes Compose inject variables into containers automatically.

options.text: Restart Docker Desktop so it rereads the `.env` file
options.why: This is how Compose works by design, not a stale cache.

explanation: The project-level `.env` file feeds variable interpolation in the Compose file: it is not copied into containers by itself. To get a value into a container, reference it from `environment` (`API_KEY=${API_KEY}`, or just `- API_KEY`), or load a file into the container with `env_file`. Keep the two ideas apart: interpolation configures the Compose file, while `environment` and `env_file` configure the container.
reference: Docker docs: Set environment variables within your container's environment

stem: The `.env` file contains `TAG=v1` and the Compose file uses `image: "shop/api:${TAG}"`. You run `TAG=v2 docker compose config`. Which image appears?

options.text: `shop/api:v1`, because the `.env` file in the project directory wins
options.why: The `.env` file is the lowest-priority interpolation source.

options.text: `shop/api:v2`, because the shell environment wins
options.why: Values exported in your shell override the `.env` file for interpolation.

options.text: `shop/api:${TAG}`, because quoted values are not interpolated
options.why: Interpolation applies to unquoted and double-quoted values.

options.text: Compose fails because `TAG` is defined in two places
options.why: Multiple sources are normal; precedence picks one.

explanation: For interpolation, Compose takes variables from your shell environment first. Next comes a file given with `--env-file`, and only then the `.env` file in the project directory. That makes `.env` a set of defaults that CI or a developer can override per command. `docker compose config --environment` shows which values Compose used.
reference: Docker docs: Variable interpolation

stem: The `.env` file contains the line `TAG=` (an empty value), and the service sets `image: web:${TAG:-stable}`. Type the image reference Compose resolves.
explanation: `${VAR:-default}` uses the default when the variable is unset or empty. `TAG` is set but empty, so the result is `web:stable`. With `${TAG-stable}`, without the colon, the default applies only when `TAG` is unset, and the result would have been `web:` with an empty tag, which is invalid.
reference: Compose file reference: Interpolation

stem: The `web` service has `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`, and `db` has a healthcheck. Put the steps of `docker compose up` in order.

options.text: Compose creates the project's default network
options.why: Shared resources come first.

options.text: Compose creates and starts the `db` container
options.why: Dependencies are created before dependents.

options.text: Compose waits until `db` reports healthy
options.why: Required by the `service_healthy` condition.

options.text: Compose creates and starts the `web` container
options.why: Only after its dependency condition is met.

explanation: Compose first creates project resources such as the default network. It then starts services in dependency order: `db` before `web`. With `service_healthy` it holds `web` back until `db`'s healthcheck passes. With the short syntax, it would start `web` as soon as the `db` container was running.
reference: Docker docs: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose

stem: The `web` service publishes `"3000:3000"`. You start it with `docker compose run web npm run dev`, but `http://localhost:3000` on the host doesn't respond. Why?

options.text: `run` always uses `network_mode: none` for one-off containers
options.why: `run` containers join the project network normally; only port publishing differs.

options.text: `run` doesn't publish the service's `ports` unless you pass `--service-ports`
options.why: One-off containers skip published ports by default to avoid clashing with the running service.

options.text: `run` ignores the command you pass on the command line and starts the service's default command instead
options.why: The command you pass replaces the service's command; that is what `run` is for.

options.text: Ports only work after `docker compose up` has created the network once
options.why: `run` creates the network itself if needed.

explanation: `docker compose run` starts a one-off container for a service. It does not publish the service's `ports` by default, so it can't collide with a container already started by `up`. Use `--service-ports` to publish them, or `-p 3000:3000` for an explicit mapping. `run` also starts the service's dependencies unless you pass `--no-deps`.
reference: Docker CLI reference: docker compose run

stem:
Given this file, which two services start with a plain `docker compose up`? (Choose two.)

```yaml
services:
  frontend:
    image: frontend
    profiles: [frontend]
  phpmyadmin:
    image: phpmyadmin
    depends_on: [db]
    profiles: [debug]
  backend:
    image: backend
  db:
    image: mysql
```

options.text: `backend`
options.why: Services without a `profiles` attribute are always enabled.

options.text: `db`
options.why: It has no profile, so it starts with every `up`.

options.text: `phpmyadmin`
options.why: It belongs to the `debug` profile, which is not enabled.

options.text: `frontend`
options.why: It belongs to the `frontend` profile, which is not enabled.

options.text: All four, because profiles only affect `docker compose run`
options.why: Profiles filter `up` too; that is their main purpose.

explanation: Services without `profiles` always start. Services with profiles start only when one of their profiles is enabled with `--profile` or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`, or when you target them by name. A plain `up` starts `backend` and `db`. Running `docker compose --profile debug up` would add `phpmyadmin`.
reference: Docker docs: Using profiles with Compose

stem: Several sources set the Compose project name. Order them from highest to lowest precedence.

options.text: The `-p` command-line flag
options.why: Highest: an explicit flag on the command.

options.text: The `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` environment variable
options.why: Next: the environment.

options.text: The top-level `name:` in the Compose file
options.why: Then the file's own declaration.

options.text: The name of the project directory
options.why: The fallback when nothing else is set.

explanation: The project name prefixes container, network and volume names, so it decides which resources belong to which environment. Compose takes it from `-p` first, then `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`, then the top-level `name:` (the last one when several `-f` files set it). The final fallback is the base name of the project directory.
reference: Docker docs: Specify a project name

stem: With the short syntax `depends_on: [db]`, Compose waits until PostgreSQL in the `db` container is ready to accept connections before it starts the dependent service.

options.text: True
options.why: Compose only waits for the `db` container to be running, not for Postgres to be ready.

options.text: False
options.why: The short syntax guarantees start order only; readiness needs `service_healthy` plus a healthcheck.

explanation: On startup, Compose waits until a dependency container is running, not until the software inside it is ready. A database often needs several seconds to initialise, so an app that connects immediately can fail. Add a healthcheck (for example `pg_isready`) and `condition: service_healthy`, and make the app retry its connection anyway.
reference: Docker docs: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose

stem:
Why does this healthcheck write `$${POSTGRES_USER}` with two dollar signs?

```yaml
healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER}"]
```

options.text: Two dollar signs tell Compose to read the value from a secret instead of the environment
options.why: Secrets are files under `/run/secrets`; `$$` has nothing to do with them.

options.text: They escape interpolation, so the container shell expands the variable at check time
options.why: `$$` becomes a literal `$` in the final config, and `CMD-SHELL` runs it through `sh`.

options.text: They make the variable mandatory, so Compose fails if it is unset
options.why: Required variables use `${VAR:?message}`, not a doubled dollar sign.

options.text: It is a typo that Compose silently fixes by dropping one of the signs
options.why: It is deliberate escaping, not error correction.

explanation: Compose interpolates `${VAR}` in the Compose file using your shell and `.env` values when it loads the project. Writing `$$` produces a literal `$`, so the string reaches the container as `pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER}`. The container's shell then expands it from the container's own environment, where `POSTGRES_USER` is set. A single `$` would be replaced at load time, probably with an empty string.
reference: Compose file reference: Interpolation (escaping)

stem: You run `docker compose up --scale api=3` and it fails. Which two settings on the `api` service would cause the failure? (Choose two.)

options.text: `container_name: api`
options.why: Compose can't create more than one container when a fixed container name is set.
Only one container can bind host port 8080, so the second and third replicas fail.
`expose` binds nothing on the host, so replicas don't conflict.

options.text: `depends_on: [db]`
options.why: Replicas can share a dependency without any conflict.

options.text: `restart: unless-stopped`
options.why: Restart policies apply per container and don't limit scaling.

explanation: Compose won't scale a service beyond one container if it sets `container_name`, because names must be unique. A fixed host port also clashes, since each replica tries to bind the same host port. Drop `container_name`, and either publish only the container port (`"8080"`, which picks an ephemeral host port) or put a load balancer or reverse proxy in front.
reference: Compose file reference: container_name and ports

stem: You merge `compose.yaml` with an override file using `-f`. Match each attribute with how Compose merges it.

options.text: The override's value replaces the base value
options.why: Single-value fields and shell commands.

options.text: Entries are appended, deduplicated by their unique key
options.why: Sequences such as published ports.

options.text: Entries are merged by the mount path inside the container
options.why: Mounts that share a target are combined.

options.text: Keys are merged, and the override wins for duplicate keys
options.why: Mappings are merged entry by entry.

explanation: Compose merges mappings key by key and appends sequences. `command`, `entrypoint` and `healthcheck.test` are exceptions: the last file replaces them instead of appending. Ports, volumes, secrets and configs are "unique resources". Ports are deduplicated by `{ip, target, published, protocol}`, and volumes, secrets and configs by their target path, so an override with the same target replaces the earlier entry.
reference: Compose file reference: Merge and override

stem: The base file publishes `"8080:80"` for `web`. The override file, merged with `-f`, lists `ports: ["9090:80"]` for `web`. Which ports end up published?

options.text: Only `9090:80`, because the override replaces the whole `ports` list
options.why: Sequences are appended, not replaced; only `command`-style fields are replaced.
The entries differ in their published port, so both survive the merge.

options.text: Only `8080:80`, because entries for the same container port are dropped
options.why: The uniqueness key includes the published port, so these are distinct entries.

options.text: Compose fails because two entries target container port 80
options.why: Publishing one container port on two host ports is valid.

explanation: Overrides can't "change" a published port by restating it: `ports` is appended, with entries deduplicated by `{ip, target, published, protocol}`. `8080:80` and `9090:80` differ, so you get both. To replace the list, use `ports: !reset []` and then add the new mapping, or keep host ports out of the base file entirely.
reference: Compose file reference: Merge and override (unique resources)

stem: The base file has `volumes: ["./src:/app"]` for `web`, and the override has `volumes: ["app-code:/app"]`. What is mounted at `/app`?

options.text: Both, stacked, with the later mount shadowing the earlier one
options.why: Compose never produces two mounts on the same target; the merge combines them.

options.text: The bind mount `./src`, because bind mounts take priority over named volumes
options.why: There is no bind-mount priority rule; the later file wins for a shared target.

options.text: The named volume `app-code`, because volume entries merge by target path
options.why: Both entries target `/app`, so the override's entry replaces the base one.

options.text: Nothing, because Compose rejects conflicting mounts with an error
options.why: A shared target is resolved by the merge rules rather than rejected.

explanation: Volume entries are keyed by their target path inside the container. When two files mount something at the same target, the later file's entry replaces the earlier one. Entries with different targets are kept from both files. `docker compose config` shows the merged result.
reference: Docker docs: Merge Compose files

stem: The base `compose.yaml` publishes `"8080:80"` for `app`. In CI you want the merged config to publish no ports at all for `app`. Which override does that?

options.text: `ports: []`
options.why: An empty sequence appends nothing, so the base entry survives.

options.text: `ports: !reset []`
options.why: The `!reset` tag clears the inherited value instead of merging with it.

options.text: `ports: ~` (a YAML null)
options.why: A plain null is not a reset; use the `!reset` tag to clear inherited values.

options.text: `expose: []`
options.why: `expose` is a different attribute; it doesn't remove published ports.

explanation: Because sequences are appended during a merge, an override can't remove inherited entries by listing fewer of them. The Compose Specification adds the YAML tag `!reset` for this. `ports: !reset []` sets `ports` back to its empty default, and `environment: { FOO: !reset null }` removes a single variable. `!override` replaces a value entirely instead of merging it.
reference: Compose file reference: Merge and override (reset value)

stem: A folder contains `compose.yaml`, `compose.override.yaml` and `compose.ci.yaml`. Running `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml up` still merges `compose.override.yaml` automatically.

options.text: True
options.why: The override file is only picked up automatically when you don't pass `-f` at all.

options.text: False
options.why: Once you list files with `-f`, Compose uses exactly those files, in that order.

explanation: The automatic `compose.override.yaml` lookup only happens when Compose discovers files on its own. If you pass `-f` (or set `COMPOSE_FILE`), it loads exactly the listed files, merged in order. This is useful in CI: dev-only bind mounts and debug ports in `compose.override.yaml` stay out of the CI configuration.
reference: Docker docs: Merge Compose files

stem: You run `docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml -f overrides/dev.yaml up` from the repository root. `overrides/dev.yaml` contains `build: ./api`. Which folder does Compose use as the build context?

options.text: `overrides/api`, relative to the file that declares it
options.why: Merged files don't resolve paths relative to themselves; they all use one base.

options.text: `deploy/api`, relative to the first Compose file's directory
options.why: All paths in merged files are resolved against the project directory set by the first `-f` file.

options.text: `./api` at the repository root, relative to where you ran the command
options.why: The current directory only applies when no project directory is derived from a file.

options.text: Compose refuses relative paths in override files
options.why: Relative paths are allowed; they just resolve against the base file's directory.

explanation: When you merge several files with `-f`, Compose resolves every relative path against the project directory. That is the directory of the first file, unless you set `--project-directory`. Override files can be fragments, so tracking a separate base per fragment would be confusing. Write all paths relative to the base file, and check the result with `docker compose config`.
reference: Docker docs: Merge Compose files (merging rules)

stem: Your project declares a named volume `pgdata` and an external network `proxy`. The `web` service bind-mounts `./src`, and an image in the project was built by Compose. Which two of these does `docker compose down -v` remove? (Choose two.)

options.text: The named volume `pgdata`
options.why: `-v` removes named volumes declared in the file.

options.text: Anonymous volumes attached to the project's containers
options.why: `-v` also removes anonymous volumes, such as those created from a Dockerfile `VOLUME` line.

options.text: The host folder `./src`
options.why: Bind mounts are host paths; Compose never deletes them.

options.text: The external network `proxy`
options.why: External resources are not managed by Compose, so `down` leaves them alone.

options.text: The image Compose built for the project
options.why: Images need `--rmi`; `-v` only affects volumes.

explanation: `down -v` adds volume removal to `down`. Named volumes declared in the `volumes` section and anonymous volumes attached to the containers go, which wipes database data. External volumes and networks, bind-mounted host folders and images are untouched. That makes `down -v` handy for resetting test databases and dangerous on a developer's real data.
reference: Docker CLI reference: docker compose down

stem: From your home folder you run `docker compose -f ~/work/shop/compose.yaml up`. A `.env` file exists both in your home folder and in `~/work/shop/`. Which one does Compose use for interpolation?

options.text: The one in your home folder, because it is the current directory
options.why: The current directory is only the fallback when no Compose file path is given.

options.text: The one in `~/work/shop/`, the directory of the first Compose file
options.why: The `.env` file is read from the project directory, which follows the first `-f` file.

options.text: Both, merged, with the home folder file winning conflicts
options.why: Compose reads a single `.env` file from the project directory.

options.text: Neither of them, because `.env` is only read when no `-f` flag is given at all
options.why: `.env` is still read; `-f` just decides where the project directory is.

explanation: Compose reads `.env` from the project directory. That is `--project-directory` if set, otherwise the directory of the first `-f` file, otherwise the current directory. So the file next to `~/work/shop/compose.yaml` is used. To use a different file, pass `--env-file`.
reference: Docker docs: Variable interpolation (ways to set variables)

stem: A Node.js service uses `docker compose watch`. Source files under `./src` should hot-reload, and a change to `package.json` should install new dependencies. Which `develop.watch` rules fit?

options.text: `sync` for both `./src` and `package.json`
options.why: Syncing `package.json` copies the file but never runs `npm install`.

options.text: `sync` for `./src`; `rebuild` for `package.json`
options.why: Source files hot-reload in place; a dependency change needs a new image.

options.text: `rebuild` for both paths
options.why: It works, but every source edit triggers a slow image rebuild and container replacement.

options.text: `sync+restart` for `./src`; `sync` for `package.json`
options.why: Restarting on every source edit defeats hot reload, and syncing `package.json` doesn't install packages.

explanation: The `sync` action copies changed files into the running container, which suits frameworks with their own hot reload. The `rebuild` action builds a new image and replaces the container, like `docker compose up --build <svc>`, so steps such as `npm install` in the Dockerfile run again. Use `rebuild` for dependency manifests and `sync` for source. Add an `ignore` for `node_modules/`, since native modules aren't portable between host and container.
reference: Docker docs: Use Compose Watch

stem: You edit `nginx.conf` on the host, and the change only takes effect after nginx restarts. No image rebuild is needed. Which Compose Watch `action` value fits best? Type the action.
explanation: `sync+restart` copies the changed file into the container and then restarts the container, so a process that reads its config only at startup picks it up. Plain `sync` would update the file without restarting nginx. `rebuild` would rebuild the image, which is unnecessary for a config file.
reference: Docker docs: Use Compose Watch (sync+restart)

stem: Which two statements about Compose Watch are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It only tracks services that have a `build` section
options.why: Watch is designed for services built from local source, not pre-built `image` services.

options.text: `ignore` patterns are relative to the rule's `path`
options.why: Ignore patterns resolve against the watched path, not the project directory.

options.text: Paths accept glob patterns such as `src/**/*.ts`
options.why: Glob patterns aren't supported in watch paths; directories are watched recursively.

options.text: It requires removing every bind mount from the service first
options.why: Watch complements bind mounts; you can use both.

options.text: The `rebuild` action keeps the old container and swaps its image
options.why: Rebuild builds a new image and replaces the running container.

explanation: Compose Watch is for services you build locally. A service defined only by `image` isn't tracked. Watched paths are relative to the project directory and are watched recursively, without glob support. `ignore` entries are relative to the rule's `path`, and `.dockerignore` rules also apply. The image needs `stat`, `mkdir` and `rmdir`, and the container user must be able to write to the target path.
reference: Docker docs: Use Compose Watch

stem: Your service sets both `image: registry.example.com/shop/api:dev` and `build: .`, with no `pull_policy`. A new teammate runs `docker compose up` and gets an old version of the API instead of one built from their checkout. Why?

options.text: Compose always prefers `build` and must be using a stale build cache
options.why: With `image` set and no pull policy, Compose tries to pull before it builds.

options.text: Compose pulls the `image` first and only builds if that image can't be found
options.why: The registry has a `:dev` image, so Compose uses it and never builds.

options.text: `image` and `build` can't be combined, so Compose ignored the `build` key
options.why: Both are allowed together: `image` names the result of the build.

options.text: The teammate's Docker Engine is too old to understand the `build` section of the file
options.why: Engine version has nothing to do with the pull-versus-build decision.

explanation: When a service has both `image` and `build`, Compose follows `pull_policy`. Without one, it tries to pull the image first and builds only if the image isn't found in the registry or local cache. The registry's `:dev` tag wins over the checkout. Use `pull_policy: build`, run `docker compose up --build`, or use a local-only tag for development.
reference: Compose Build Specification: Using build and image

stem: `web` has `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy, restart: true } }`. In which case does Compose restart `web` because of that `restart: true`?

options.text: Whenever `db` crashes and the Docker daemon restarts it automatically under its own restart policy
options.why: Automatic restarts by the container runtime are explicitly excluded.

options.text: When a Compose operation such as `docker compose restart db` restarts or recreates `db`
options.why: It covers updates and restarts that Compose itself performs on the dependency.

options.text: Whenever `db` reports unhealthy at any point while both are running
options.why: Healthchecks gate startup; they don't make Compose restart dependents later.

options.text: Never, because `restart: true` only applies when used with Swarm
options.why: It is a Compose feature, added in Compose 2.17.

explanation: `restart: true` inside a `depends_on` entry tells Compose to restart the dependent service after it updates or restarts the dependency through a Compose operation. Examples are `docker compose restart db`, or `up` recreating `db` after a config change, so `web` can re-establish connections. It doesn't react to the daemon restarting a crashed container under its `restart:` policy.
reference: Compose file reference: depends_on (long syntax)

stem: Match each interpolation expression with its behaviour.

options.text: Default when unset or empty
options.why: Colon form checks for emptiness.

options.text: Default only when unset
options.why: Without the colon, an empty value counts as set.

options.text: Error when unset or empty
options.why: Stops Compose with the given message.

options.text: Replacement text when set and non-empty
options.why: Otherwise it resolves to an empty string.

explanation: Compose follows shell-style parameter expansion. The colon forms treat an empty value like an unset one: `:-` falls back to a default, `:?` aborts with an error, and `:+` substitutes replacement text only when the variable is set and non-empty. The forms without a colon (`-`, `?`, `+`) only check whether the variable is set.
reference: Docker docs: Variable interpolation (interpolation syntax)

stem: The image sets `ENV VALUE=1.5`, the project `.env` file contains `VALUE=1.3`, and `VALUE` is not set in your shell. The service has no `environment` or `env_file`. What is `VALUE` inside the container after `docker compose run --env VALUE web env`?

options.text: `1.5`, because the image's `ENV` applies when Compose sets nothing
options.why: Compose does set something here: `--env VALUE` forwards a value.

options.text: `1.3`, because `--env VALUE` forwards the value from the `.env` file
options.why: With no shell value, the forwarded name resolves from `.env`.

options.text: Empty, because `--env VALUE` without `=` clears the variable
options.why: A bare name forwards a value; it doesn't clear it.

options.text: Unset, because `.env` only feeds interpolation and never reaches containers
options.why: True on its own, but `--env VALUE` explicitly forwards the resolved value.

explanation: `--env VALUE` with no value means "forward this variable". Compose resolves it from the shell first, then from `.env`. The shell has no `VALUE`, so `1.3` from `.env` is used, and it overrides the image's `ENV VALUE=1.5`. This matches row 7 of Docker's precedence table. If the shell had `VALUE=1.4`, the container would get `1.4`.
reference: Docker docs: Environment variables precedence (advanced example)

stem: The image sets `ENV VALUE=1.5`, your shell exports `VALUE=1.4`, and `.env` contains `VALUE=1.3`. The service declares `environment: [VALUE]`, a bare name with no value. What does the container see after `docker compose up`?

options.text: `1.5`, because a bare name means "keep the image default"
options.why: A bare name forwards a value from Compose's environment; it doesn't defer to the image.

options.text: `1.3`, because `.env` is the project-level source for Compose
options.why: `.env` is only used when the shell doesn't set the variable.

options.text: `1.4`, because the shell value is forwarded and wins over `.env`
options.why: A bare entry takes the value Compose resolves, and the shell beats `.env`.

options.text: Empty, because a bare name with no `=` sets the variable to an empty string
options.why: An entry without `=` forwards a value; it isn't an assignment to empty.

explanation: An `environment` entry with only a name tells Compose to pass through the value it resolves for that variable. Your shell environment takes precedence over the `.env` file, so the container gets `1.4`, overriding the image's `ENV`. With no shell value, it would get `1.3` from `.env`. This is rows 10 and 11 of Docker's precedence table.
reference: Docker docs: Environment variables precedence (advanced example)

stem: An `env_file` sets `VALUE=1.6`, `environment` sets `VALUE=1.7`, the image has `ENV VALUE=1.5`, and you run `docker compose run --env VALUE=1.8 web env`. Which value does the container get?

options.text: `1.7`, because the Compose file's `environment` attribute is authoritative
options.why: `environment` beats `env_file` and the image, but not the command line.

options.text: `1.6`, because `env_file` is loaded last
options.why: `env_file` has lower precedence than `environment` and `--env`.

options.text: `1.5`, because image defaults can't be overridden by `run`
options.why: Every Compose source overrides image `ENV` defaults.

options.text: `1.8`, because `run --env` has the highest precedence
options.why: The command-line value overrides `environment`, `env_file` and the image.

explanation: For the container environment, `docker compose run --env` comes first, then the `environment` attribute, then `env_file`, then the image `ENV`. An explicit `--env VALUE=1.8` therefore wins over everything in the Compose file. This is row 15 of Docker's precedence table, and it lets you override a single run without editing the file.
reference: Docker docs: Environment variables precedence

stem: `.env` contains `DB_PASSWORD=` (empty), and you want `docker compose up` to refuse to start whenever the password is missing or blank. Which reference does that?

options.text: `${DB_PASSWORD?Set DB_PASSWORD}`
options.why: Without the colon, only an unset variable fails; an empty value passes through.

options.text: `${DB_PASSWORD:?Set DB_PASSWORD}`
options.why: The colon form treats an empty value like an unset one and aborts with the message.

options.text: `${DB_PASSWORD:-}` with an empty default
options.why: That supplies an empty default, so Compose always continues.

options.text: `$${DB_PASSWORD}`
options.why: Doubling the dollar sign escapes interpolation, so Compose never checks the value.

explanation: Required-variable syntax comes in two forms. `${VAR?msg}` fails only if `VAR` is unset. `${VAR:?msg}` also fails when it is set but empty. A line like `DB_PASSWORD=` in `.env` sets the variable to an empty string, so only the colon form catches it. Use `:?` for credentials and other values that must never be blank.
reference: Compose file reference: Interpolation

stem: Repository `infra/compose.yaml` defines `db` with `build: ./postgres`, where `infra/postgres/` exists. The app's `app/compose.yaml` needs that `db` service too. Which approach builds `db` from `infra/postgres` without rewriting paths?

options.text: Run `docker compose -f app/compose.yaml -f infra/compose.yaml up`
options.why: With `-f` merging, `./postgres` resolves against `app/`, the first file's directory.

options.text: Add `include: [../infra/compose.yaml]` to the app's Compose file
options.why: Each included file keeps its own project directory for resolving relative paths.

options.text: Use `extends` on every service in `infra/compose.yaml`
options.why: `extends` copies service config, but paths still need care and it is per service, not per file.

options.text: Symlink `infra/compose.yaml` into `app/` and use the auto-loaded override
options.why: A symlink doesn't change path resolution, and the override name wouldn't match.

explanation: `include` loads each listed file as its own Compose application model, with its own project directory for relative paths, then copies its resources into the current project. `-f` merging resolves every path against the first file's directory, which would look for `app/postgres`. Use `include` to compose independently owned Compose files, and `-f` overlays for environment-specific tweaks to one application.
reference: Compose file reference: include

stem: A CI job runs integration tests against a Compose stack on a shared runner. Several pipelines may run at the same time. Which three practices make the job reliable? (Choose three.)

options.text: Give each run its own project name, for example `-p ci-$BUILD_ID`
options.why: Distinct project names isolate containers, networks and volumes between parallel runs.

options.text: Bring dependencies up with `docker compose up -d --wait` before running tests
options.why: `--wait` blocks until services are running or healthy, so tests don't start too early.

options.text: Always finish with `docker compose down -v`, even when tests fail
options.why: Removing volumes gives the next run a clean database, and cleanup prevents leaks.

options.text: Rely on the short `depends_on` syntax so the database is ready
options.why: Short syntax only orders startup; it doesn't wait for readiness.

options.text: Publish fixed host ports so the test runner can find each service
options.why: Fixed host ports collide between parallel runs on the same machine.

options.text: Use `docker compose down` without `-v` so data carries over between runs
options.why: Leftover data makes tests order-dependent and flaky.

explanation: Project names namespace every resource, so unique names per build stop parallel jobs from sharing containers or volumes. `up --wait` waits for services to be running or healthy, which with good healthchecks removes startup races. A cleanup step with `down -v` in an "always" block resets state. Avoid fixed host ports on shared runners: run the tests in a container on the project network, or let Docker pick ports.
reference: Docker CLI reference: docker compose up (--wait)

stem: You change an environment variable on `db` and run `docker compose up -d`. Compose recreates `db`, and afterwards the `api` service, which kept running, logs connection errors until it is restarted. What explains this?

options.text: Recreating `db` renamed the service, so `api` can no longer resolve `db`
options.why: The service name stays the same; only the container is replaced.

options.text: `db` got a new IP address, and `api`'s pooled connections still point at the old one
options.why: DNS resolves the name to the new container, but existing connections aren't moved.

options.text: Compose attaches a recreated container to a brand-new network, isolating `db` from the running `api`
options.why: The recreated container rejoins the same project network.

options.text: Compose always stops dependents when it recreates a dependency
options.why: Compose doesn't restart `api` unless `depends_on` has `restart: true`.

explanation: When Compose recreates a container, the new one joins the network under the same service name but usually a different IP address. Open connections to the old container are closed, and clients must look up the name again and reconnect. Connection pools that cache addresses or don't retry show errors until restarted. Make clients reconnect with backoff, or add `restart: true` to the dependency so Compose restarts `api` too.
reference: Docker docs: Networking in Compose (updating containers)

stem:
Given this file, you run `docker compose run --rm db-migrations` with no profiles enabled. Which two services start? (Choose two.)

```yaml
services:
  backend:
    image: backend
  db:
    image: mysql
  db-migrations:
    image: backend
    command: myapp migrate
    depends_on: [db]
    profiles: [tools]
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: [tools]
```

options.text: `db-migrations`
options.why: Targeting a service by name runs it even though its profile isn't enabled.

options.text: `db`
options.why: Declared dependencies of the targeted service are started too.

options.text: `adminer`
options.why: It shares the `tools` profile but isn't targeted, and the profile isn't enabled.

options.text: `backend`
options.why: `run` starts only the target and its dependencies, not every default service.

options.text: None, because a service in a disabled profile can't be run
options.why: Explicitly targeting a service activates it regardless of its profile.

explanation: When you name a service on the command line, Compose runs it even if its profile isn't enabled. It also starts the service's `depends_on` dependencies. Other services in the same profile, such as `adminer`, stay stopped unless they are targeted or the profile is enabled. `run` also doesn't start unrelated services like `backend`.
reference: Docker docs: Using profiles with Compose (auto-starting profiles)

stem: `app` depends on `migrate` with `condition: service_completed_successfully`. A bad migration makes `migrate` exit with code 1. What happens on `docker compose up`?

options.text: `app` starts anyway once `migrate` has exited, whatever the exit code
options.why: That would ignore the condition; the dependency must succeed.

options.text: `app` is not started, and Compose reports that its dependency failed
options.why: The condition is unmet because the exit code isn't 0.

options.text: Compose retries `migrate` until it exits with 0, then starts `app`
options.why: `depends_on` doesn't retry dependencies; restarts come only from a restart policy.

options.text: `app` starts in a degraded state with its health set to unhealthy
options.why: There is no degraded start; the dependent simply isn't started.

explanation: `service_completed_successfully` requires the dependency to run to completion with exit code 0. If it fails, the condition can never be met, so Compose doesn't start the dependent service and reports the dependency failure. The app never runs against a half-migrated schema. Fix the migration, or inspect it with `docker compose logs migrate`.
reference: Docker docs: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose

stem: The same variable is set in several places that feed interpolation of a Compose file. Order the sources from highest to lowest precedence.

options.text: The variable exported in your shell environment
options.why: Highest priority for interpolation.

options.text: A file passed with `--env-file`
options.why: Used instead of the default `.env`.

options.text: The `.env` file in the project directory
options.why: Lowest of these three.

explanation: For interpolation, Compose first uses your shell environment. It then uses a file given with `--env-file`, and, if none is given, the `.env` file in the project directory. This makes `.env` a place for defaults that can be overridden per command or per CI job. Container environment precedence (`run --env`, `environment`, `env_file`, image `ENV`) is a separate list.
reference: Docker docs: Variable interpolation

stem: The base file publishes `"8080:80"` for `web`. The override, merged with `-f`, lists `ports: ["8080:80", "9090:80"]`. Which ports are in the merged configuration?

options.text: `8080:80`, `8080:80` and `9090:80`, with Compose failing on the duplicate
options.why: Identical entries share a unique key, so they merge instead of duplicating.

options.text: Only `8080:80` and `9090:80` from the override, with the base list dropped
options.why: The base list isn't dropped; the merge appends and deduplicates.
The repeated mapping has the same unique key and merges; the new one is appended.

options.text: Only `9090:80`, because the repeated entry cancels the base one
options.why: Merging never removes entries without `!reset`.

explanation: Ports are a unique resource keyed by `{ip, target, published, protocol}`. Merging appends override entries that don't violate uniqueness and merges those that share a key. The repeated `8080:80` merges with the base entry, and `9090:80` is added, giving two mappings. Run `docker compose config` to see exactly what Compose will apply.
reference: Compose file reference: Merge and override (unique resources)

stem: A Compose file in folder `shop/` declares a named volume `pgdata` for Postgres. After someone renames the folder to `shop-api/` and runs `docker compose up`, the database is empty. What happened?

options.text: Renaming the folder deleted the volume's data from disk
options.why: The old volume and its data still exist; nothing was deleted.

options.text: The project name changed, so Compose created a new volume `shop-api_pgdata`
options.why: Volume names are prefixed with the project name, which defaults to the folder name.

options.text: Postgres ignores named volumes the first time a new container starts, so it re-initialised
options.why: Postgres initialises the data directory only when the volume it mounts is empty.

options.text: Named volumes are scoped to a container, and Compose made a new container
options.why: Volumes outlive containers; that is why they hold data.

explanation: Compose prefixes networks and named volumes with the project name, which defaults to the base name of the project directory. After the rename, the project is `shop-api`, so Compose created an empty `shop-api_pgdata`. The old `shop_pgdata` volume is still on disk. Pin the project with a top-level `name: shop` (or `-p`), or declare the volume with an explicit `name:` or as `external`.
reference: Docker docs: Specify a project name
